title: Autopsy and Portrait
premise: Ulyana Yarrow, archivist and unofficial fixer for the cathedral parish, accepts a strange retainer: a nervous lawyer pays him to prove that the murder at the center of an upcoming trial hasn't happened — because the supposed victim, a homeless organist, keeps sending letters. Digging through the locked crypt's records, Ulyana finds evidence the letters are real, written by a witness the diocese declared dead years ago to bury a scandal. As the trial nears, church officials, the real killer, and the lawyer's own clients close in, and Ulyana must smuggle the living 'dead man' into the courtroom. The case ends with the witness testifying, the killer convicted, and Ulyana — who built his life on invisibility — choosing at last to be seen, signing his name to the cathedral's restored records.
about_author: Edmund Blackwood is the pen name of a former parish records clerk who spent a decade cataloguing deaths, baptisms, and the paperwork of quiet disappearances. They write mysteries about people the institutions would rather forget.

chapters.title: The Retainer
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. A lawyer named Corvin arrives at the archive with an envelope of cash and an impossible request: prove the murder never happened. Ulyana, who prides himself on closable cases, accepts against his better judgment. The emotional beat is wary curiosity — the first crack in a carefully maintained invisibility.

chapters.title: Letters from a Dead Man
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Examining the letters supposedly written by murdered organist Tomas Rehl, Ulyana finds handwriting matching parish records from eight years ago — when Rehl was declared dead in a fire. The beat is mounting unease: the dead, in Ulyana's experience, do not write.

chapters.title: The Locked Crypt
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, with a tense scene from the crypt keeper's perspective. Ulyana picks the lock on the crypt and finds Rehl's coffin empty, its records altered in the diocese's hand. The beat is transgressive thrill — crossing a line he can't uncross.

chapters.title: Everyone Swears
chapters.summary: Multiple short POV vignettes: the dean, the sexton, a grieving sister — all insisting Rehl is dead, some too smoothly. Ulyana maps the lies like an archive. The beat is claustrophobia: an entire institution aligned on a single falsehood.

chapters.title: The Organist's Room
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Following Rehl's old haunts, he finds a squatter who remembers the organist and a hidden cache of documents implicating a diocesan benefactor in an embezzlement Rehl witnessed. The beat is grief — the city's forgotten keeping its true records.

chapters.title: What Corvin Isn't Saying
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. He discovers Corvin's firm also defends the accused killer — the retainer is a trap to find and destroy the witness. Confronted, Corvin reveals he took the case to sabotage it from within. The beat is betrayal curdling into uneasy alliance.

chapters.title: Ash Wednesday
chapters.summary: Rehl's POV, first time. The witness, living rough and half-believing his own death, watches Ulyana find him and refuses to testify — the church buried him once already. The beat is hollowed-out despair meeting stubborn compassion.

chapters.title: The Trial Begins
chapters.summary: Alternating Ulyana and Corvin POV. The prosecution's case collapses as the 'victim's' absence is weaponized; the diocese moves to have Rehl legally confirmed dead, which would end everything. The beat is a clock ticking — days left, nowhere safe.

chapters.title: The Man in the Gallery
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, climax. Smuggling Rehl into the courtroom through the cathedral's connected passages, Ulyana is intercepted by the dean and the benefactor's men; the crypt keeper, choosing conscience over institution, opens the last door. Rehl takes the stand. The beat is breathless sacrifice rewarded.

chapters.title: Autopsy and Portrait
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, resolution. The killer is convicted, the benefactor exposed, and the diocese offers Ulyana silence in exchange for returning the stolen records. Instead he restores them publicly, entering Rehl's true death-date — none — into the archive. The beat is quiet belonging: a man who catalogued the unseen finally signs his own name.
